name: Olga Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a feed truck for Brennan's Mill, delivering animal feed to farms across the valley. It's a bulk blower, which means the truck blows the feed up a pipe into the farm's silo. I do six or seven farms a day, down lanes barely wider than the truck, and I'm still learning not to overfill the bins. My dad drove milk tankers on these same roads for thirty years.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my fiancé Piotr in a rented cottage at the edge of the village, near St Michael's church. He's a farmhand on the Ashby dairy farm. We're getting married next summer, and the wedding money is basically all we've got, about three weeks of bills if it came to it. I don't have any of those AI things, I barely use the internet except for the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I never trusted it in the first place. Down at the mill the men would say the same. I don't go online, so it'd be over a cup of tea in somebody's farm kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the farms are my worry, not AI. Two of my regular farms sold up this year, and Brennan's Mill has already cut one truck. If more farms go, there's less feed to deliver, and I'm the newest driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do my rounds well, so the farmers ask for me. I'd ask old Mr Brennan if I can learn the mixing side at the mill too, so I'm useful for more than driving. And we'd keep the wedding small, in the church hall rather than the hotel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit tired of worrying. Nothing to do with computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think the farms are closing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Prices, mostly, and the young ones don't want the life. The supermarkets pay them next to nothing for milk. It's not machines, it's money, and nobody in a city office seems to care about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're the newest driver. What happens if the mill cuts another truck?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it's me, last in, first out. Mr Brennan's fair, but he can't keep me out of kindness. I'd probably end up on the chicken factory line twenty miles away, which I'd hate.

say: I **never trusted** AI in the first place.
I'd say it over tea in a **farm kitchen**, not online.
The men at the mill would **agree** with me.
think: The **farms closing** worries me, not AI.
Brennan's already **cut a truck**, and I'm the newest driver.
**Last in, first out** could send me to the chicken factory line.
do: Do my rounds well so **farmers ask for me**.
Ask Mr Brennan to learn the **mixing side** at the mill.
Keep the **wedding small**, in the church hall.
feel: **Uneasy** and tired of worrying about things unrelated to computers.
S0.quote: Two of my regular farms sold up this year, and Brennan's Mill has already cut one truck.
fieldNote: Real pressure is **farm closures** shrinking the feed trade.
**Last in, first out** puts her job at risk regardless of AI.
Traditional values show in a **church wedding** and loyalty to the mill owner.

steps.text: Keep doing the valley feed rounds carefully so farmers ask for her
Ask Mr Brennan to teach her the feed-mixing side
Move the wedding reception to the church hall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's for the city folk with desks, not for us. You can't send a computer down Ashby Lane, the farm road to the dairy, with ten tonnes of feed. I'd say that at church, at the mill, anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I worry about the mill office. Mrs Doyle takes all the orders by phone and knows every farmer's bins by heart. If the orders go on an app, the old farmers will hate it, and some will go to the big feed firms instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd just carry on. If the mill brought in a computer for the orders, I'd let someone else learn it and keep to my driving. Piotr and I would save what we could for the wedding and not change much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, like when the weather turns. I don't like change, and this is a lot of change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the mill lost customers this way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not Mr Brennan, he'd be doing what he must. The big feed firms, maybe, and the people who make it all so cheap that the small mills can't keep up. It's the market, I suppose, but it doesn't feel fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever use an app yourself, if the mill asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to, to keep the job, yes. Piotr would show me, he's better with his phone. But I'd do it grumbling.

say: AI is for **city folk** with desks.
You can't send a computer down **Ashby Lane** with ten tonnes of feed.
think: **Mrs Doyle** takes orders by phone and could be replaced by an app.
Old farmers might **move to big firms** if the ordering changes.
do: **Carry on** with my driving as before.
Let someone else learn any **ordering system**.
Save what we can for the **wedding**.
feel: **Uneasy**, like the weather turning, and disliking so much change.
S1.quote: You can't send a computer down Ashby Lane, the farm road to the dairy, with ten tonnes of feed.
fieldNote: Her driving is safe for now, but the **mill's customers** may drift away.
Free-market view softened by a sense that small firms **lose unfairly**.
Resistant: would use an app only **under pressure**, with Piotr's help.

steps.text: Carry on with the daily feed rounds as before
Put wedding savings aside every payday
Wait and see what ordering system the mill brings in

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong and it shouldn't be allowed to happen that fast. People need work, not handouts. I'd say it after church to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be terrified. By 2031 a robot truck could do my rounds, and Piotr's milking work could go to robots too. That's both of us, with a new marriage and maybe a baby on the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving as long as Brennan's keeps me. I'd ask my dad's old friends if there's anything on the farms that needs a person, like hoof trimming or fencing. We'd probably move in with my parents after the wedding to save the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd pray a lot, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad he got out at the right time. He'd say there's always work for people who'll get their hands dirty. I'd want to believe him, but I'm not sure he's right this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your wedding or family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still get married, that's not changing. We'd wait on a baby, which breaks my heart a bit, because my mum had me at 24 and I wanted to be a young mum too.

say: It's **wrong** to let it happen that fast.
I'd say it **after church** to anyone listening.
think: By **2031** a robot truck could do my rounds.
Piotr's **milking work** could go too, so it's both of us.
do: Keep **driving** as long as Brennan's keeps me.
Ask Dad's friends about **farm jobs** needing a person.
**Move in** with my parents after the wedding to save rent.
S2.quote: We'd wait on a baby, which breaks my heart a bit, because my mum had me at 24 and I wanted to be a young mum too.
fieldNote: Both she and her fiancé work in **hands-on rural jobs** that robots could take.
Postponing a **baby** is the most painful cost she names.
Traditional response: lean on **family and faith**, not government.
Has no plan beyond **asking around** among her father's friends.

steps.text: Keep the Brennan's feed rounds as long as the mill keeps her
Move in with her parents after the wedding to save rent
Put off having a baby until work feels safer
Ask her dad's farming friends about hands-on farm jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, it's too fast and it isn't right. But I'd also say our village has to look after its own. I'd talk to the vicar about it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, eight years to the robots means I'd be 35. That's still young enough to start again, but I don't know what I'd start at. I've never been good at school things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Brennan to put me on the mixing floor, since a mill still needs someone who knows feed. Piotr would try for the herdsman job at Ashby, the one that looks after the cows' health. We'd save harder after the wedding and stay in the cottage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still scared, but there's a bit of room to breathe. Like a long hill instead of a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not good at school things. Would you do a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if it's hands-on, with someone showing me. Not on a computer. My cousin did a farrier apprenticeship, shoeing horses, and loved it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help your village most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keeping the farms going. If the farms stay, the mill stays, and so does the pub and the school. That's what I'd want the government to think about, not cheques in the post.

say: It's **too fast** and it isn't right.
Our village has to **look after its own**.
I'd talk to **the vicar** about it.
think: At **35** I'm young enough to restart, but I don't know at what.
I've never been good at **school things**.
do: Ask to move to the **mixing floor** at Brennan's.
Back Piotr going for the **herdsman job** at Ashby.
**Save harder** after the wedding and stay in the cottage.
feel: **Scared but breathing**, like a long hill rather than a cliff.
S3.quote: If the farms stay, the mill stays, and so does the pub and the school.
fieldNote: More time helps, but she still expects to **lose driving** and has no clear trade.
Only open to **hands-on learning**, not computer courses.
Thinks in terms of the **whole village**, not just her job.

steps.text: Ask Mr Brennan to move her onto the mill's mixing floor
Save harder after the wedding and stay in the rented cottage
Talk to the vicar about help for village families

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is fair, and folk should use it. I'd tell young ones at church to learn a proper trade. I still wouldn't go online about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, I'd be 40, maybe with a child at school by then. Ten years means I can have the family first and worry about the job later. The thinking AI in 2036 won't touch a feed truck, but the robots three years after would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and get better at it, because that's my wage now. After the wedding, we'd try for a baby. In a few years I'd look at the farrier apprenticeship my cousin did, or something like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can live with it. The money now is still the hard part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So the long warning changes the baby plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, completely. With two years, we'd wait on a baby, but with ten, we'd go ahead and trust that we'll manage, like my parents did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hard part about money now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cottage rent went up again, and the truck makes my back ache so I can't do extra shifts. If the mill cuts a truck before any robots come, I'm still the one who goes. That's the worry that's real today.

Young ones should learn a **proper trade**.
I still wouldn't **go online** about it.

feel: **Uneasy** but able to live with it, with money the hard part.
S4.quote: With two years, we'd wait on a baby, but with ten, we'd go ahead and trust that we'll manage, like my parents did.
fieldNote: The warning time directly changes her **family plans**.
Still anxious because the **mill cutting a truck** could hit her any year.

steps.text: Keep driving the feed truck and improve on the narrow lanes

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes my truck and Piotr's cows at the same time. What would help is apprenticeships for hands-on trades, paid, near home, so we don't have to move to a city.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the village. If the robots take the farm work, it's not just jobs, it's the pub, the school, the church. A place can die even if the people are fed.

headlineQuote: A place can die even if the people are fed.
portrait: Olga, 27, drives a **feed blower truck** to valley farms for Brennan's Mill, following her father onto these roads.
She's engaged to farmhand Piotr, with a **church wedding** next summer and about three weeks' savings.
Traditional and wary of tech, she **never uses AI** and prefers work over handouts.
Her deepest fear is **both jobs** going together, which would make her delay a baby.
She thinks in terms of the **whole village**: farms, mill, pub and school.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which takes her truck and Piotr's dairy work together.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid hands-on apprenticeships** near home, so they don't move to a city.
